questions.q:
Consider the following initial rate data for the reaction $A + B \rightarrow C$:

| Trial | $[A]_0$ (M) | $[B]_0$ (M) | Initial Rate (M/s) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | 0.10 | 0.10 | $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| 2 | 0.20 | 0.10 | $4.0 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| 3 | 0.10 | 0.20 | $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ |

What is the reaction order with respect to reactant **A**?
questions.explain: Compare Trial 1 and Trial 2. $[B]$ is constant (0.10 M). $[A]$ doubles ($0.10 \rightarrow 0.20$). The rate doubles ($2.0 \rightarrow 4.0$). Since rate $\propto [A]^1$, the reaction is First order with respect to A. Source: OpenStax 12.3 Method of Initial Rates.

questions.q:
Refer to the data table in the previous question (Trials 1, 2, and 3).

| Trial | $[A]_0$ (M) | $[B]_0$ (M) | Initial Rate (M/s) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | 0.10 | 0.10 | $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| 3 | 0.10 | 0.20 | $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ |

What is the reaction order with respect to reactant **B**?
questions.explain: Compare Trial 1 and Trial 3. $[A]$ is constant (0.10 M). $[B]$ doubles ($0.10 \rightarrow 0.20$). The rate remains unchanged ($2.0 \times 10^{-3}$). Since the rate is independent of $[B]$, the reaction is Zero order with respect to B. Source: OpenStax 12.3 Method of Initial Rates.

questions.q:
Using the data below for the reaction $2NO + O_2 \rightarrow 2NO_2$, determine the **overall** reaction order.

| Trial | $[NO]_0$ (M) | $[O_2]_0$ (M) | Initial Rate (M/s) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | 0.010 | 0.010 | $2.5 \times 10^{-5}$ |
| 2 | 0.020 | 0.010 | $1.0 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| 3 | 0.010 | 0.020 | $5.0 \times 10^{-5}$ |
questions.explain:
Step 1: Compare Trials 1 & 2 ($[O_2]$ const). $[NO]$ doubles, Rate quadruples ($2.5 \rightarrow 10.0$). Order wrt NO = 2.
Step 2: Compare Trials 1 & 3 ($[NO]$ const). $[O_2]$ doubles, Rate doubles ($2.5 \rightarrow 5.0$). Order wrt $O_2$ = 1.
Overall order = $2 + 1 = 3$. Source: OpenStax 12.3 Method of Initial Rates.

questions.q:
For the reaction $X + Y \rightarrow Z$, the rate law is determined to be $\text{Rate} = k[X][Y]^2$. Using the data from Trial 1 below, calculate the value of the rate constant $k​$.

| Trial | $[X]_0$ (M) | $[Y]_0$ (M) | Rate (M/s) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | 0.20 | 0.10 | $4.0 \times 10^{-4}$ |
questions.explain:
Rearrange the rate law: $k = \frac{\text{Rate}}{[X][Y]^2}$.
Substitute values: $k = \frac{4.0 \times 10^{-4}}{(0.20)(0.10)^2} = \frac{4.0 \times 10^{-4}}{(0.20)(0.01)} = \frac{4.0 \times 10^{-4}}{0.002} = 0.20$. Units for 3rd order are $\text{M}^{-2}\text{s}^{-1}$. Source: OpenStax 12.3 Rate Laws.

questions.q:
Determine the correct rate law for the reaction $A + B \rightarrow Products$ based on the following data:

| Exp | $[A]$ (M) | $[B]$ (M) | Rate (M/min) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | 0.10 | 0.10 | 0.005 |
| 2 | 0.30 | 0.10 | 0.045 |
| 3 | 0.10 | 0.20 | 0.005 |
questions.explain:
Compare 1 & 2: $[B]$ const, $[A]$ triples ($0.1 \rightarrow 0.3$), Rate x9 ($0.005 \rightarrow 0.045$). $3^m = 9$, so $m=2$ (Order wrt A = 2).
Compare 1 & 3: $[A]$ const, $[B]$ doubles, Rate unchanged. Order wrt B = 0.
Rate law: Rate = $k[A]^2$. Source: OpenStax 12.3 Rate Laws.

questions.q:
Consider the data below. How does the rate change when the concentration of $B​$ is doubled (holding $A​$ constant)?

| Run | $[A]$ | $[B]$ | Rate |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | 1.0 | 1.0 | $R​$ |
| 2 | 1.0 | 2.0 | $4R$ |
options: The rate increases by a factor of 8.
questions.explain: Directly from the table: When $[A]$ is constant and $[B]$ goes from 1.0 to 2.0 (doubles), the rate goes from $R​$ to $4R$. This indicates the reaction is second order with respect to B ($2^2 = 4$). The change is a quadrupling. Source: OpenStax 12.3 Rate Laws.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: For a reaction $2A + B \rightarrow C$, the rate law is found to be $\text{Rate} = k[A]$. Which statement is true about the effect of changing $[B]$?
options: Changing $[B]$ has no effect on the rate.
The reaction cannot proceed if $[B]$ is low.
questions.explain: The rate law $\text{Rate} = k[A]$ implies that the reaction is zero order with respect to B. Therefore, the concentration of B does not appear in the rate equation, and changing it has no effect on the rate (provided B is present). Source: OpenStax 12.3 Rate Laws.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: If a reaction is determined to be **second order overall**, what are the units of the rate constant $k​$? (Assume time in seconds and concentration in mol/L).
questions.explain: Rate = $k[Concentration]^2$. Units: $(\text{M/s}) = k \cdot (\text{M})^2$. Thus $k = (\text{M/s}) / \text{M}^2 = \text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$. Since $\text{M} = \text{mol/L}$, $M^{-1} = \text{L/mol}$. So units are $\text{L mol}^{-1} \text{s}^{-1}$. Source: OpenStax 12.3 Table 12.1.

questions.explain: Compare Exp 2 and Exp 4. $[A]$ is constant (0.2), $[B]$ is constant (0.1). $[C]$ doubles ($0.1 \rightarrow 0.2$). Rate changes from $4.0 \times 10^{-4}$ to $1.6 \times 10^{-3}$ (which is $16 \times 10^{-4}$). Ratio: $16/4 = 4$. Since doubling conc quadruples rate ($2^n=4$), order is 2. Source: OpenStax 12.3 Rate Laws.

questions.q: A reaction has the rate law $\text{Rate} = k[A]^2$. If $[A]$ is $0.10 \text{ M}$ and the rate is $5.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ M/s}$, what will be the rate if $[A]$ is increased to $0.30 \text{ M}$?
questions.explain: Tripling the concentration ($0.10 \rightarrow 0.30$) for a second-order reaction increases the rate by a factor of $3^2 = 9$. New Rate = $9 \times (5.0 \times 10^{-3}) = 45 \times 10^{-3} = 4.5 \times 10^{-2} \text{ M/s}$. Source: OpenStax 12.3 Rate Laws.
